extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory, constitutional scholars, and historians studying federalism and the durability of the American Union
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and factors for judging the stability and likely duration of a federal union, especially the United States in the 19th century; draws distinctions between types of governmental affairs and examines geographical, economic, social, and institutional forces that promote or threaten unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorization of governmental affairs (national / provincial / mixed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish objects which are national by their nature (affecting the nation as a whole), provincial (affecting only localities), and mixed (affecting all citizens but not necessarily requiring national uniformity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: war and diplomacy are national; a municipal budget is provincial; civil and political rights are mixed. How affairs are classed affects whether they should be entrusted to the central or provincial government and thus influences the balance of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of mixed affairs to the central government
rubrics_metrics.description: When the national (federal) government is invested with the right of regulating mixed affairs, it acquires preponderating influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the central government regulates matters that are partly general and partly local, not only are its rights extensive, but the rights it does not possess exist by its sufferance, making provincial governments vulnerable to loss of prerogatives and tending toward centralization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of mixed affairs to provincial governments
rubrics_metrics.description: If provincial governments control mixed affairs, the preponderant force lies with the provinces rather than the nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When provinces assume control of mixed affairs, the national government may be stripped of privileges necessary to its existence, creating a tendency toward dismemberment of the union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin and composition of sovereign authority (individuals vs preorganized bodies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the sovereign power is formed by union of separate individuals or by preexisting political bodies affects which level of government will dominate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If sovereign authority arose from individuals, the national government naturally governs more; if from preorganized political bodies (states), provincial governments retain considerable power and influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative strength and felt influence of federal vs provincial governments
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the federal government's undertakings are vast, provincial governments' actions are more immediately felt by citizens and thus sustain greater loyalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provincial governments are incessant in daily affairs (regulating liberty, property, justice) while the central government handles grand, less-felt interests (national greatness, foreign policy), so citizens tend to attach more to their State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governmental proximity and accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The physical and institutional proximity of provincial governments to citizens strengthens provincial authority and attachment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal government is remote; provincial governments are within reach and respond to small appeals, fostering stronger local loyalty and political activity centered on the State rather than the Union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patriotic sentiment directed at State rather than Union
rubrics_metrics.description: The Union's lack of a clear, circumscribed object for patriotic feeling makes citizens more likely to feel patriotism toward their State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The State is identified with soil, property, domestic affections, recollections and hopes; patriotism often being an extension of individual egoism therefore centers on the State and not the Union, weakening national cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral tendencies of governments in constitutional disputes (command vs reason)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provincial governments tend to act boldly and command when asserting claims; the federal government tends to parley, argue, and temporize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If doubts arise about constitutional limits, states press their claims energetically; the federal government appeals to interests and glory and is slower to coerce, which favors provincial resistance and weakens central authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical geography and natural barriers
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence or absence of natural barriers (mountains, rivers) affects the ease of separation and the strength of mutual intercourse among provinces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the Alleghanies are not an effective barrier—low elevation, passes, and rivers create easy intercourse—so lack of natural barriers in inhabited regions supports union rather than separation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial extent and population distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Large territorial extent and the direction of population growth (e.g., toward the northwest) affect political power distribution and can be a danger to union if contrary interests arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extent can be prejudicial if different provinces develop opposing interests; conversely, if interests are not opposed, a large territory can enhance prosperity through internal interchange. Rapid growth in one direction shifts power and produces passions from sudden changes of fortune.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal economic interests between regions
rubrics_metrics.description: Differing regional economies (agricultural South, commercial/industrial North, mixed West) create reciprocal dependencies that bind the union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The North needs raw materials and markets from South/West; South/West need commercial resources and naval protection provided by the North/Union. Such reciprocal interests reduce incentives for separation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial ties and necessity of external trade
rubrics_metrics.description: Commerce makes the states effectively neighbors of foreign nations and creates a material interest in remaining united to present collective strength and avoid fragmentation into separate economic units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dissolution would create inland custom-houses, hinder river navigation, and impede exploration and exchange across the continent; present unity facilitates large markets and trade benefits all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military capacity and absence of a standing army
rubrics_metrics.description: A federal government's ability to coerce or enforce allegiance is limited by distances and usually by the absence of a standing army, making enforcement of federal will over states difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without standing armies, a central government is ill-prepared to seize opportunities to conquer resistance; long distances and dispersed population amplify enforcement difficulties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for common defense (navy) as material incentive
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain regions derive direct political and economic advantages (e.g., protection of maritime exports) from a common defense maintained by the union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Southern and Western states rely on a national navy and foreign communication; these needs incline them to support the Union to secure protection and market access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual ties and uniformity of opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Shared ideas, information, and uniformity of opinion among citizens are intellectual bonds that promote union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intellectual ties (information, democratic liberties) create affinities that help hold diverse regions together; the absence of such uniformity increases danger to union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct characters and passions of regional populations
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in character, customs, and passions across regions (e.g., Northern vs Southern attitudes, especially on slavery) create dangers to union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral and social differences can generate conflicting political passions that threaten cohesion; Tocqueville cites slavery as a central divisive passion that culminated in secession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether any State is indispensable to the Union
rubrics_metrics.description: If no single State's existence or prosperity is wholly dependent on the Union, States are unlikely to make great personal sacrifices to maintain it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the Union is advantageous but not indispensable to any State, none will be disposed to great sacrifices to preserve it, reducing collective will to resist dismemberment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unequal distribution of union benefits leading to domination
rubrics_metrics.description: If some States exclusively enjoy the main advantages of the union, they may be willing to support strong federal action and even use federal authority to dominate others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The federal government could then act with borrowed power; the union's authority would be exercised in the interest of particular States rather than the confederation as a whole, undermining the original federative principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical traditions and preexisting provincial institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Long-standing local traditions, customs, and institutions condition citizens' attachments and may be at variance with constitutional distributions of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a compact nation divides sovereignty, traditions may give more influence to the central government than legislation intended; conversely, when preorganized states form a confederation, provincial traditions sustain local authority and impede centralization.
